**Coordinate space.** Let $C:=\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{3}$, whose elements are written $(t,x)$ with $t\in\mathbb R$ and $x=(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})\in\mathbb R^{3}$. The Euclidean inner product and norm on the second factor are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]; addition and scalar multiplication on $C$ are componentwise, and $I_{3}$ is the identity matrix of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]].

**The transformations.** For a quadruple $\theta=(b,a,v,R)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{3}\times\mathbb R^{3}\times SO(3)$ ([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]) define the map $g_{\theta}:C\to C$ by

$$g_{(b,a,v,R)}(t,x):=\bigl(t+b,\ Rx+v\,t+a\bigr),$$

where $Rx$ and $vt$ are the usual matrix–vector products with $R=(R_{ij})$ and with the column vectors $x,v,a$. The four components of $\theta$ are called the **time shift** $b$, the **spatial translation** $a$, the **boost velocity** $v$ and the **rotation** $R$, and $\theta$ is called the **parameter quadruple** of $g_{\theta}$. Write

$$G:=\bigl\{g_{(b,a,v,R)}:(b,a,v,R)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{3}\times\mathbb R^{3}\times SO(3)\bigr\}$$

for the set of all these maps and $\Theta:=\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{3}\times\mathbb R^{3}\times SO(3)$ for the parameter set. The elements of $G$ are the **Galilean transformations of the coordinate space**, and the assignment $\theta\mapsto g_{\theta}$ is the **parameter map**.

**Elementary readings.** For $R=I_{3}$ and $v=0$ the map $g_{(b,a,0,I_{3})}$ is the pure time-and-space translation $(t,x)\mapsto(t+b,x+a)$; for $b=0$, $a=0$ and $R=I_{3}$ it is the pure boost $(t,x)\mapsto(t,x+vt)$; and for $b=0$, $a=0$, $v=0$ it is the rotation $(t,x)\mapsto(t,Rx)$ acting only on the spatial factor. The time coordinate of $g_{\theta}(t,x)$ depends only on $t$ and $b$, in accordance with the absolute-time convention of the model that consumes this definition.

**What is and is not asserted.** This definition introduces the maps and names their parameters. It asserts no property of the parameter map (such as injectivity), no closure of $G$ under composition or inversion, no continuity, smoothness or differentiability of the maps, and no physical interpretation: whether these maps describe changes between inertial frames of a physical model is a separate, explicitly adopted assumption of the physics items that consume this definition. The group structure of $G$ is proved in the group lemma of this page, and the units in which the parameters are read are fixed by the model's unit conventions, not here.

In the notation of [[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]:

1. $I_3\in SO(3)$, and for all $R,S\in SO(3)$ the matrices $RS$ and $R^{\mathsf T}$ again lie in $SO(3)$; moreover $\det R=1$, $R$ is invertible, and its inverse is $R^{\mathsf T}$, so also $RR^{\mathsf T}=I_3$.
2. Consequently $SO(3)$ is a subgroup of the general linear group $GL_3(\mathbb R)$ ([[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]], [[cor-general-linear-group-is-a-group]]).

Let $M_3(\mathbb R)$ be the set of $3\times3$ matrices over $\mathbb R$ ([[def-matrix-space]]), with identity $I_3$ and product as in [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], transpose $R^{\mathsf T}$ as in [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]], and determinant $\det R$ as in [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]].

The **orthogonal group** and the **special orthogonal group** are the subsets

$$O(3):=\{R\in M_3(\mathbb R):R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3\},\qquad SO(3):=\{R\in M_3(\mathbb R):R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3\ \text{and}\ \det R=1\}.$$

Equivalently $SO(3)=O(3)\cap\{R:\det R=1\}$. Elements of $SO(3)$ are called **rotations**. The identification of $M_3(\mathbb R)$ with the function space $\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ and hence with $\mathbb R^9$ is the one of [[def-matrix-space]]; when $M_3(\mathbb R)$ is regarded as a metric or topological space, this is always the Euclidean metric of that identification.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

derivations.claim: [Injectivity] Assume $g_{(b,a,v,R)}=g_{(b',a',v',R')}$. Evaluating at $(0,0)$ and comparing first coordinates gives $b=b'$. Evaluating at $(0,x)$ then gives $Rx+a=R'x+a'$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^{3}$; at $x=0$ this gives $a=a'$, and after subtracting, $(R-R')x=0$ for every $x$, which for $x=e_{1},e_{2},e_{3}$ compares the three columns of the matrix $R-R'$ and gives $R=R'$. Evaluating at $(t,0)$ then gives $vt+a=v't+a'$ for every real $t$; subtracting the known $a=a'$ and taking $t=1$ gives $v=v'$. Hence $\theta=\theta'$.

[Composition] For every $(t,x)\in C$, applying first $g_{(b_{1},a_{1},v_{1},R_{1})}$ and then $g_{(b_{2},a_{2},v_{2},R_{2})}$ gives $\bigl(t+b_{1}+b_{2},\ R_{2}(R_{1}x+v_{1}t+a_{1})+v_{2}(t+b_{1})+a_{2}\bigr)$. By the linearity and associativity identities of [L3] this equals $\bigl(t+(b_{1}+b_{2}),\ (R_{2}R_{1})x+(R_{2}v_{1}+v_{2})t+(R_{2}a_{1}+v_{2}b_{1}+a_{2})\bigr)$, which is $g_{\theta_{3}}(t,x)$ for $\theta_{3}:=(b_{1}+b_{2},\,R_{2}a_{1}+v_{2}b_{1}+a_{2},\,R_{2}v_{1}+v_{2},\,R_{2}R_{1})$; and $R_{2}R_{1}\in SO(3)$ by [L2], so $\theta_{3}\in\Theta$ and the composite is Galilean with the displayed parameters. Taking the second quadruple to be $(0,0,0,I_{3})$ makes the composite equal $g_{\theta_{1}}$ by [L2], and taking the first to be $(0,0,0,I_{3})$ makes it equal $g_{\theta_{2}}$; hence $g_{(0,0,0,I_{3})}$ is the identity map of $C$, and the composite lies in $G$.

[Inverse] Let $\theta=(b,a,v,R)$ and $\eta:=(-b,\,-R^{\mathsf T}(a-vb),\,-R^{\mathsf T}v,\,R^{\mathsf T})$; by [L2] $R^{\mathsf T}\in SO(3)$, so $\eta\in\Theta$. For $(t',x')\in C$ put $t:=t'-b$ and $x:=R^{\mathsf T}\bigl(x'-v(t'-b)-a\bigr)$. Then $t+b=t'$, and $Rx+vt+a=R\,R^{\mathsf T}\bigl(x'-v(t'-b)-a\bigr)+v(t'-b)+a=x'$ by $RR^{\mathsf T}=I_{3}$ of [L2]; hence $g_{\theta}(t,x)=(t',x')$ and $g_{\theta}$ is surjective. Expanding $x$ gives $x=R^{\mathsf T}x'+(-R^{\mathsf T}v)t'+\bigl(-R^{\mathsf T}(a-vb)\bigr)=g_{\eta}(t',x')$, so $g_{\theta}\circ g_{\eta}$ is the identity of $C$. If $g_{\theta}(t_{1},x_{1})=g_{\theta}(t_{2},x_{2})$ then $t_{1}=t_{2}$ from the first coordinate, and $R(x_{1}-x_{2})=0$ from the second, giving $x_{1}=x_{2}$ because $R$ is invertible by [L2]; so $g_{\theta}$ is injective, and with surjectivity it is a bijection.

[Two-sided inverse] By step 1.2 the composite $g_{\theta}\circ g_{\eta}$ has parameters $\bigl(-b+b,\ R a_{\eta}+v b_{\eta}+a,\ R v_{\eta}+v,\ RR^{\mathsf T}\bigr)$ with $(b_{\eta},a_{\eta},v_{\eta},R_{\eta})=\eta$, so its components are $0$, $R\bigl(-R^{\mathsf T}(a-vb)\bigr)+v(-b)+a=-(a-vb)-vb+a=0$, $R(-R^{\mathsf T}v)+v=-v+v=0$ and $RR^{\mathsf T}=I_{3}$; hence $g_{\theta}\circ g_{\eta}=g_{(0,0,0,I_{3})}$, the identity of $C$ by step 1.2. This proves clause 2 with the displayed inverse.

[Subgroup] By steps 1.2 and 2.1 the set $G$ contains the identity of the bijection group of $C$ and is closed under composition and inversion; by step 1.1 the parameter map is injective, and every $g_{\theta}$ is a bijection by steps 1.3 and 2.1. Therefore $G$ is a subgroup of the group of all bijections of $C$ under composition, and clauses 1-4 hold.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix
$\hbar>0$ and an integer $d\ge1$, and work in the complex Hilbert space
$L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with inner product
$\langle f,g\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R^d}f\overline g$ linear in the first
argument ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]],
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]).

**Weak derivatives.** For $f\in L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ and
$j\in\{1,\dots,d\}$, say that the $j$-th weak derivative of $f$ exists in
$L^2$ when there is a class $g\in L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with
$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}f\,D_j\varphi=(-1)\int_{\mathbb R^d}g\,\varphi \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d),$$
where $D_j\varphi$ is the classical partial derivative and the pairing is
bilinear without conjugation ([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]).
Such a $g$ is unique as an $L^2$ class
([[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]]); write $D_jf:=g$.
The Sobolev space $W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ is the set of classes
$f\in L^2$ for which $D_1f,\dots,D_df$ all exist in $L^2$, and
$W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ is the set of $f\in W^{1,2}$ with
$D_jf\in W^{1,2}$ for every $j$, with $D_jD_kf$ written for the iterated
derivative ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]).

**(a) Position operators.** For $j\in\{1,\dots,d\}$ define
$$D(Q_j):=\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C):\ x\mapsto x_jf(x)\in L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)\},\qquad (Q_jf)(x):=x_jf(x).$$
Thus $Q_jf$ is the class of the pointwise product with the $j$-th coordinate
function.

**(b) Momentum operators.** For $j\in\{1,\dots,d\}$ define
$$D(P_j):=\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C):\ D_jf\text{ exists in }L^2\},\qquad P_jf:=-i\hbar\,D_jf .$$

Both $Q_j$ and $P_j$ are densely defined $\mathbb C$-linear operators in
$L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$: for $Q_j$ the compactly supported smooth
classes lie in the domain because $x_j$ is bounded there, and for $P_j$ they
lie in the domain because their classical derivatives are weak derivatives in
$L^2$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]). For a class
$f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ one has $Q_jf=x_jf$ and
$P_jf=-i\hbar\,\partial_jf$ pointwise. The self-adjointness of these operators
and their Fourier representation are proved in
the companion self-adjointness lemma on this page, not
asserted here; for $d=1$ the domain $D(P)$ of the single momentum operator
coincides with $W^{1,2}(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open,
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, and let $u:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ have real
and imaginary parts of class $C^k$. For each multi-index
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$ with $|\alpha|\le k$, the componentwise classical
derivative $\partial^\alpha u$ is locally integrable and is the weak
derivative $D^\alpha u$. By the uniqueness lemma, it represents the unique
locally integrable weak-derivative class. For $\alpha=0$, this says
$D^0u=u$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the assertion is vacuous: there is only the zero
class and every displayed test identity is zero.

Assume countable choice. If $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$, then $x^\alpha\partial^\beta f\in L^p$ for every $1\le p\le\infty$ and every $\alpha,\beta$. Its norm is bounded by a finite sum of Schwartz seminorms.

Fix an integer $n\ge1$. With the complex smooth-function convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]] and multi-indices of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], define
$$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|,\qquad \mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)=\{f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C):p_{\alpha\beta}(f)<\infty\text{ for all }\alpha,\beta\}.$$
The zero multi-index gives $x^0=1$ and $\partial^0f=f$. These are actual smooth functions, not equivalence classes. The notation $C_c^\infty$ uses the support convention in [[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]].

Pointwise differentiation is linear; thus $p_{\alpha\beta}(f+g)\le p_{\alpha\beta}(f)+p_{\alpha\beta}(g)$ and $p_{\alpha\beta}(cf)=|c|p_{\alpha\beta}(f)$. In particular this set is a complex vector space and each $p_{\alpha\beta}$ is a seminorm. The zero function belongs to it. Since $p_{00}(f)=0$ forces $f(x)=0$ for every $x$, the family separates functions. No choice principle is needed.

For $n\ge1$, there exists $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$, $\chi=1$ on $|x|\le1$, and $\chi=0$ on $|x|\ge2$. For $R>0$, $\chi_R(x)=\chi(x/R)$ satisfies $\partial^\beta\chi_R(x)=R^{-|\beta|}(\partial^\beta\chi)(x/R)$. The construction requires no choice.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \varphi(x)\,dx = 1. $$

For $\varepsilon > 0$, define

$$ \varphi_\varepsilon(x) := \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon) \qquad(x \in \mathbb{R}^n). $$

The family $(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is the **mollifier family
generated by $\varphi$**.

Assume countable choice, let $n\ge1$, and use Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^n$. Translation $\tau_hf(x)=f(x-h)$ is an isometry of complex $L^p$ for $1\le p\le\infty$ and depends norm-continuously on $h$ for $p<\infty$.

For complex $K\in L^1$ and $f\in L^p$, the convolution
$$(K*f)(x)=\int K(y)f(x-y)\,dy$$
exists absolutely a.e., defines a measurable class independent of representatives, and satisfies $\|K*f\|_p\le\|K\|_1\|f\|_p$.

If $K_\varepsilon\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ satisfy
$$\int K_\varepsilon=1,\qquad M:=\sup_{\varepsilon>0}\|K_\varepsilon\|_1<\infty,\qquad \int_{|y|\ge\delta}|K_\varepsilon(y)|\,dy\longrightarrow0\quad(\delta>0),$$
then $K_\varepsilon*f\to f$ in $L^p$ for $p<\infty$, and uniformly for $f\in C_0(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. For fixed $K\in L^1$, $K*f\in C_0$ when $f\in C_0$. These assertions allow complex and sign-changing kernels. In particular $K_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-n}K(x/\varepsilon)$ is such an approximate identity whenever $K\in L^1$ and $\int K=1$.

If $\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R)$ has mass one, $\rho_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-n}\rho(x/\varepsilon)$, and $f$ is complex locally integrable, then $\rho_\varepsilon*f$ is smooth and
$$\partial^\alpha(\rho_\varepsilon*f)=(\partial^\alpha\rho_\varepsilon)*f.$$
A compactly supported input gives a compactly supported output. No general $L^\infty$ translation-continuity or approximate-identity convergence is asserted.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: [Schwartz invariance and domains] Let $f\in\mathcal S$. By [L2], $x_jf$ and $\partial_kf$ are Schwartz and in $L^2$; by [L1], $f\in D(Q_j)\cap D(P_k)$, $Q_jf=x_jf\in\mathcal S$, and $P_kf=-i\hbar\partial_kf\in\mathcal S$. This proves (a) and ensures both products in (b) are defined.

[The position operators have Schwartz cores] Fix $j$ and $f\in D(Q_j)$, and define $f_n=\chi_n f$ using [L3]. Since $\chi_n(x)\to1$ for each fixed $x$ and $|\chi_n|\le1$, dominated convergence applied to $|f_n-f|^2$ and $|x_j(f_n-f)|^2$ gives $\|f_n-f\|_2+\|x_jf_n-x_jf\|_2\to0$. Each $f_n$ is supported in $|x|\le2n$. For fixed $n$, let $g_{n,\epsilon}=\rho_\epsilon*f_n$; by [L4] it is smooth, compactly supported in $|x|\le2n+2\epsilon$, and $\|g_{n,\epsilon}-f_n\|_2\to0$. For $0<\epsilon\le1$, $|x_j|\le2n+2$ on both supports, so $\|x_j(g_{n,\epsilon}-f_n)\|_2\le(2n+2)\|g_{n,\epsilon}-f_n\|_2$. Choose $\epsilon_n\le1$ so the latter $L^2$ error is below $n^{-2}$. Then $g_{n,\epsilon_n}\in C_c^\infty\subseteq\mathcal S$ and converges to $f$ in the graph norm of $Q_j$. Thus $\mathcal S$ is a core for $Q_j$.

[Classical product rule and commutator] Since $x_jf\in\mathcal S$, its classical derivative is its weak derivative by [L1]. By [L5], $D_k(x_jf)=\partial_k(x_jf)=\delta_{jk}f+x_j\partial_kf$. Therefore $P_kQ_jf=-i\hbar(\delta_{jk}f+x_j\partial_kf)$, while $Q_jP_kf=-i\hbar x_j\partial_kf$. Subtraction yields $(Q_jP_k-P_kQ_j)f=i\hbar\delta_{jk}f$, proving (b) directly on Schwartz representatives.

[The momentum operators have Schwartz cores] Fix $k$ and $f\in D(P_k)$; put $f_n=\chi_nf$. For every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty$, the weak derivative identity for $f$ applied to $\chi_n\varphi$ gives $\int f_n\partial_k\varphi=-\int(\chi_nD_kf+(\partial_k\chi_n)f)\varphi$, so $D_kf_n=\chi_nD_kf+(\partial_k\chi_n)f\in L^2$. Dominated convergence gives $f_n\to f$ and $\chi_nD_kf\to D_kf$ in $L^2$, while [L3] gives $\| (\partial_k\chi_n)f\|_2\le n^{-1}\|\partial_k\chi\|_\infty\|f\|_2\to0$; hence $f_n\to f$ in the graph norm of $P_k$. For fixed $n$, let $g_{n,\epsilon}=\rho_\epsilon*f_n$. For a test function $\varphi$, change variables and apply the weak-derivative identity inside the convolution integral: $\int g_{n,\epsilon}(x)\partial_k\varphi(x)\,dx=\int\rho_\epsilon(y)\int f_n(z)\partial_k\varphi(z+y)\,dz\,dy=-\int(\rho_\epsilon*D_kf_n)(x)\varphi(x)\,dx$. The interchange is valid by [L6], so $\partial_kg_{n,\epsilon}=\rho_\epsilon*D_kf_n$ as a weak derivative; since $g_{n,\epsilon}$ is smooth, it is also its classical derivative. Both $g_{n,\epsilon}\to f_n$ and $\partial_kg_{n,\epsilon}\to D_kf_n$ in $L^2$ by [L4]. Choose $\epsilon_n>0$ so both errors are below $1/n$. Then $g_{n,\epsilon_n}\in C_c^\infty\subseteq\mathcal S$ and converges to $f$ in the graph norm of $P_k=-i\hbar D_k$. Thus $\mathcal S$ is a core for $P_k$. Since $j,k$ were arbitrary, the proof establishes the common-core assertion in the Statement and completes (a) and (b).

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following kinematics and one-particle model. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), which are the choice hypotheses of the cited operator suppliers.

**(i) Spacetime and frames.** The model reads its events and frames in the Newtonian arena of [[def-nrqm-framework-newtonian-spacetime]], with inertial frames and frame changes as in [[def-nrqm-framework-inertial-frames]]: the frame changes are the Galilean transformations of [[def-nrqm-framework-galilei-transformations]], and their composition is governed by the group law of [[lem-nrqm-framework-galilei-transformations-form-a-group]]. These frames are global coordinate charts, not observer congruences and not time-varying basis fields. The parameters of a frame change are read in the units fixed by [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]].

**(ii) Apparatus motion.** The macroscopic constituents of preparations and apparatus are described by the classical trajectories of [[def-nrqm-framework-classical-apparatus-trajectories]]; a quantum particle of the model is not assigned a worldline between preparations and detections.

**(iii) One-particle state space.** For one particle of spin label $s\in\{0,\tfrac12,1,\tfrac32,\dots\}$ and mass parameter $m>0$, the model uses the state space

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following statement of isolated autonomous dynamics. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), which are the choice hypotheses of the cited spectral and group suppliers.

**(i) Energy operator.** An **isolated autonomous system** of the sector has a declared **energy operator** $H_{\mathrm{op}}:D(H_{\mathrm{op}})\subset H\to H$ that is self-adjoint ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]) and a declared energy unit in which its spectral coordinate is read. The energy operator is part of the model specification of the system; for a massive particle it is fixed by the kinematics postulate P5, and singular or unbounded model Hamiltonians require their own self-adjointness statements.

**(ii) Evolution.** The time evolution of the model is the strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group
$$U(t):=\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{i}{\hbar}tH_{\mathrm{op}}\Bigr)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R),\qquad U(t+s)=U(t)U(s),\quad U(t)^{*}=U(t)^{-1},$$
defined by the spectral calculus of the self-adjoint generator ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], [[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]], [[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]], [[def-strongly-continuous-one-parameter-unitary-group]]). The energy unit enters the argument of the exponential so that $H_{\mathrm{op}}t/\hbar$ acts in the dimensionless spectral variable.

**(iii) State evolution.** A vector state evolves continuously, $\psi(t):=U(t)\psi(0)$ for every $\psi(0)\in H$, and the Schroedinger equation
$$i\hbar\,\frac{d}{dt}\psi(t)=H_{\mathrm{op}}\psi(t)$$
holds in the norm-differentiable sense exactly for initial vectors $\psi(0)\in D(H_{\mathrm{op}})$, where the derivative is the norm limit of the difference quotients; for other vectors the equation is not asserted, although the evolution remains continuous. A density-operator preparation evolves as $\rho(t)=U(t)\rho(0)U(t)^{*}$, which is a density operator for every $t$ and satisfies $\operatorname{tr}\rho(t)=1$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]]).

The general unbounded time-dependent case requires a separate existence and domain theorem of its own and is not adopted by this postulate; the driven-dynamics page states its own assumptions for the models it treats.

**(v) Open systems.** A non-unitary evolution of the reduced description of a system coupled to an environment is an extension obtained from an explicitly chosen environment model and a declared reduction, not a replacement for clause (ii); no environment model is adopted by this postulate.

**(vi) Status.** Clauses (i)-(v) are adopted assumptions of the isolated-system idealization. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix
$\hbar>0$, $m>0$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ and
$I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be nonempty open sets, let $V:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be
continuous and let $\psi:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb C$ be such that $\psi$,
$\partial_t\psi$ and all spatial partial derivatives $\partial_j\psi$,
$\partial_k\partial_j\psi$ ($j,k\in\{1,2,3\}$) exist and are continuous on
$\Omega\times I$, and
$$i\hbar\,\partial_t\psi(x,t)=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\Delta\psi(x,t)+V(x)\psi(x,t) \qquad\text{for every }(x,t)\in\Omega\times I,$$
where $\nabla\psi:=(\partial_1\psi,\partial_2\psi,\partial_3\psi)$ is the spatial
gradient and $\Delta\psi:=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_j\partial_j\psi$ is the
classical Laplacian on $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]],
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]). Define the **current**
$$j(x,t):=\frac{\hbar}{m}\operatorname{Im}\bigl(\overline{\psi(x,t)}\,\nabla\psi(x,t)\bigr)\in\mathbb R^3 .$$
Then:

(a) *pointwise continuity equation.* For every $(x,t)\in\Omega\times I$,
$$\partial_t|\psi|^2(x,t)+\operatorname{div}j(x,t)=0,$$
where the divergence is the classical one of the $C^1$ field
$x\mapsto j(x,t)$ ([[lem-divergence-and-curl-are-linear-and-obey-the-scalar-product-rules]]);

(b) *integrated balance.* If $D\subseteq\Omega$ is a bounded open set with
$C^1$ boundary and $\overline D\subseteq\Omega$
([[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-c-one-euclidean-domains]]), then
$t\mapsto\int_D|\psi(x,t)|^2dx$ is differentiable on $I$ with
$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_D|\psi(x,t)|^2dx=-\int_{\partial D}j(x,t)\cdot n(x)\,dS ,$$
$n$ the outward unit normal;

(c) *global conservation under domination.* If $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, if there
is $g\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ with $|\psi(x,t)|^2\le g(x)$ for almost every $x$
and every $t\in I$, and if
$$\lim_{R\to\infty}\ \sup_{t\in I}\ \int_{\{|x|=R\}}|j(x,t)|\,dS=0,$$
then, for all $s,t\in I$ such that the closed interval joining $s$ and $t$
is contained in $I$,
$$\|\psi(\cdot,s)\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3)}^2=\|\psi(\cdot,t)\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3)}^2;$$

(d) *norm conservation from unitary dynamics.* If $K$ is a self-adjoint
operator on a complex Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ and
$\psi(t):=e^{-itK/\hbar}\psi_0$ for some $\psi_0\in\mathcal H$, then
$\|\psi(t)\|=\|\psi_0\|$ for every $t\in\mathbb R$
([[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]],
[[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]]).

Assertion (d) is independent of the smooth local model of (a)-(c); no
interpretation of $|\psi|^2$ as a measured counting rate is asserted.

**Inertial frames.** Fix the arena $(V,\tau,g,A)$ of [[def-nrqm-framework-newtonian-spacetime]]. An **inertial frame** of the framework is an adapted chart

$$F=\bigl(o,u,(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})\bigr)$$

of that arena in the sense of [[def-cm-affine-time-space]]: an event $o\in A$ (the **spatial and time origin** of the frame), a vector $u\in V$ with $\tau(u)=1$ (the frame's **time vector**), and an ordered $g$-orthonormal positively oriented basis $(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})$ of $K$ (the frame's **spatial triad**). The associated **frame coordinates** are the functions $(t,x):A\to\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{3}$ of [[lem-cm-adapted-coordinates-exist-and-are-unique]], defined by $p=o+t(p)u+\sum_{i}x_{i}(p)e_{i}$.

**What kind of object a frame is.** A frame is a coordinate chart of $A$: a bijection of $A$ with $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{3}$ carrying the affine structure, and in particular a global chart, not a local one. It is deliberately not an observer congruence (no family of curves indexed by spatial position, no four-velocity field) and not a time-varying orthonormal basis field: the triad $(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})$ is a fixed basis of $K$ and the time vector $u$ is fixed once the frame is chosen. A time-dependent family of bases or a congruence of observers is a different geometric object, and statements about them are not statements about frames unless a separate construction relates them.

**Allowed changes of frame.** Let $F$ and $F'$ be two inertial frames with coordinates $(t,x)$ and $(t',x')$. The **change of frame** from $F$ to $F'$ is the bijection of $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{3}$ that sends the $F$-coordinates of an event to its $F'$-coordinates. By clause 1 of [[lem-cm-adapted-charts-and-galilean-transformations]] there are $b\in\mathbb R$, $a,v\in\mathbb R^{3}$ and $R\in SO(3)$ ([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]) with

$$t'=t+b,\qquad x'=Rx+vt+a;$$

that is, the change of frame is the Galilean transformation $g_{(b,a,v,R)}$ of [[def-nrqm-framework-galilei-transformations]] applied to the coordinates. The class of transformations between inertial frames is therefore the set $G$ of the Galilean transformations, which by [[lem-nrqm-framework-galilei-transformations-form-a-group]] is a group of bijections of the coordinate space: the composite of two frame changes is again a frame change, and the inverse of a frame change is a frame change. The parameters are the time shift $b$, the spatial translation $a$, the boost velocity $v$ and the rotation $R$ of the two frames.

**Conventions.** The spatial triad of every frame is positively oriented for the fixed orientation of $K$ used in the definition of adapted charts, so all frame changes have $R\in SO(3)$ rather than $R\in O(3)$ with negative determinant. The reading of the coordinates in seconds and metres, and the physical meaning of the parameters as measured quantities, are fixed by the unit conventions recorded on this page; no measured value of any parameter is asserted here.

**Status.** This definition fixes the frames and the class of frame changes of the model. It asserts no property of forces or of the motion of any body, selects no distinguished frame, and makes no empirical claim. The adoption of these frames as the frames of the physical model, together with the reading of apparatus motion as classical, is part of the kinematics postulate of this page.

**(a) Dimensions.** Write $\ell$, $\tau$, $\mu$, $\vartheta$ for the four independent dimension symbols of length, duration, mass and electric charge. A **dimension** is an element of $\mathbb Z^{4}$, written $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\vartheta^{d}$; products and inverses of dimensions are componentwise addition and negation, and the dimensionless dimension $\ell^{0}\tau^{0}\mu^{0}\vartheta^{0}$ is abbreviated $1$. The conventions assign to each quantity of the framework a dimension $[X]$, subject to $[XY]=[X][Y]$, $[X/Y]=[X][Y]^{-1}$ and $[dX/du]=[X][u]^{-1}$, with sums meaningful only between quantities of equal dimension, in which case the sum carries that dimension. These are consistency requirements on the conventions, not laws of nature.

**(b) Reference units.** The **metre** (m), **second** (s), **kilogram** (kg) and **coulomb** (C) are the reference units of length, duration, mass and charge; a quantity of dimension $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\vartheta^{d}$ is expressed in the unit $\mathrm m^{a}\mathrm s^{b}\mathrm kg^{c}\mathrm C^{d}$. Coordinates of an inertial frame are read with the time coordinate $t$ in seconds, $[t]=\tau$, and the spatial coordinates $x_{i}$ in metres, $[x_{i}]=\ell$; slice distances of the arena are read in metres.

**(c) Defining constants of the current SI.** The framework keeps $\hbar$ explicit. In the current SI the constants $h$, $c$ and $e$ are exact defining constants, with the values $h=6{,}626\,070\,15\times10^{-34}$ J s, $c=2{,}99792458\times10^{8}$ m s$^{-1}$ and $e=1{,}602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}$ C, and $\hbar:=h/(2\pi)$; the vacuum permeability $\mu_{0}$ is experimentally determined and $\varepsilon_{0}:=(\mu_{0}c^{2})^{-1}$. These are unit-convention statements of the SI, not measurements reported by this framework; $c$ enters the framework only through the separate radiation assumptions adopted on their own pages, not in the nonrelativistic spacetime of [[def-nrqm-framework-newtonian-spacetime]].

**(d) Dimensions and types of the framework's quantities.** The dimension map is fixed on the following quantities.

1. State quantities: a position wave function of a system with $d$ spatial dimensions and $r$ internal components is an almost-everywhere equivalence class in $L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ with dimension $\ell^{-d/2}$, its norm $\|\psi\|$ is dimensionless, and an abstract normalized state and the density operators of the state postulate are dimensionless.
2. Probability: the outcome probability $\mu(B)$ of the observable postulate is a dimensionless number; a position density $|\psi|^{2}$ has dimension $\ell^{-d}$; a momentum wave function normalized against $\mathrm d^{d}p$ has dimension $(\mu\ell\tau^{-1})^{-d/2}$; an amplitude for a finite outcome is a dimensionless complex number, while an amplitude read against a detector coordinate carries the square-root of the inverse of the detector measure.
3. Frame parameters ([[def-nrqm-framework-galilei-transformations]]): $[b]=\tau$, $[a_{i}]=\ell$, $[v_{i}]=\ell\tau^{-1}$ and $[R_{ij}]=1$.
4. Mechanical quantities: action $[\hbar]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$; energy and the Hamiltonian eigenvalues $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$; momentum $\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$; position components $\ell$; angular momentum and spin $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$; mass $\mu$; velocity of a free spinless model $\ell\tau^{-1}$; force $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$; a real potential energy $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$.
5. Probability current: $j$ has dimension $\ell^{1-d}\tau^{-1}$; it is a probability flux, not a charge flux.
6. Electric quantities of the model parameters: charge has dimension $\vartheta$; a magnetic moment has dimension $\ell^{2}\vartheta\tau^{-1}$, equivalently $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{2}=\mathrm J\,\mathrm T^{-1}$, and a gyromagnetic parameter $\gamma$ in the relation $\boldsymbol\mu=\gamma\mathbf S$ has dimension $\mu^{-1}\vartheta$, equivalently $\mathrm s^{-1}\mathrm T^{-1}$; these quantities appear only in the model assumptions that introduce them.
7. Statistical quantities: a mean has the dimension of its outcome coordinate, a variance the square of it and a standard deviation it; a mean, variance or higher moment exists only when the corresponding moment of the outcome probability is finite, so a symbolic average is not a number unless that integrability is established. Angles and phases are dimensionless under the radian convention.
8. Quantities of later extension assumptions - radiation frequencies and energies, electric dipole moments, cross sections, temperatures and entropies - are declared with their dimensions and units by the items that introduce those assumptions, under the rules fixed here; they are not part of the present list.

**(e) Conventions only.** No numerical value of any model parameter is fixed by this item: no mass, charge, spin label, potential or measured constant is asserted, and natural-unit shorthand (for example setting $\hbar=1$ or $c=1$) is read as an abbreviation for the corresponding SI-dimensioned statement with the constant restored.

derivations.claim: The coordinates have $[t]=\tau$ and $[x_{i}]=\ell$, so a three-dimensional position wave function has $[\psi]=\ell^{-3/2}$, its squared modulus has $[|\psi|^{2}]=\ell^{-3}$, and the product $|\psi|^{2}\mathrm d^{3}x$ is dimensionless, as required of a probability density.

For the operators of [L1], $[Q_{j}\psi]=[x_{j}][\psi]=\ell\cdot\ell^{-3/2}=\ell^{-1/2}=[\psi]\cdot\ell$ gives $[Q_{j}]=\ell$, and $[P_{k}\psi]=[\hbar]\cdot[\partial_{k}\psi]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}\cdot\ell^{-5/2}=\mu\ell^{-1/2}\tau^{-1}=[\psi]\cdot\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$ gives $[P_{k}]=\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$; the commutator identity is consistent, since $[Q_{j}P_{k}]=\ell\cdot\mu\ell\tau^{-1}=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}=[\hbar]=[i\hbar\delta_{jk}]$.

For the Hamiltonian of [L2], the kinetic term acts as $[(-\hbar^{2}/2m)\Delta\psi]=\mu^{2}\ell^{4}\tau^{-2}\mu^{-1}\ell^{-2}\ell^{-3/2}=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}\ell^{-3/2}=[E][\psi]$, and the potential term satisfies $[V\psi]=[V][\psi]$ with $[V]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}=[E]$; both terms therefore carry the dimension of energy times wave function, as required for their sum to define an operator.

The Schroedinger equation is dimensionally consistent: $[i\hbar\partial_{t}\psi]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}\cdot\tau^{-1}\cdot\ell^{-3/2}=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}\ell^{-3/2}=[H_{\mathrm{op}}\psi]$, and the phase $H_{\mathrm{op}}t/\hbar$ of the evolution operator is dimensionless because $[E][t][\hbar]^{-1}=1$.

The current of [L3] has $[j]=[\hbar][m]^{-1}[|\psi|^{2}][\nabla\psi][\psi]^{-1}=\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}\cdot\ell^{-3}\cdot\ell^{-1}=\ell^{-2}\tau^{-1}$, which is $\ell^{1-d}\tau^{-1}$ for $d=3$: a probability flux per unit area and time, not a charge current.

The expression $mv\cdot x/\hbar$ in [L4] is dimensionless, $[mv\cdot x]/[\hbar]=\mu\ell\tau^{-1}\cdot\ell\cdot(\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1})^{-1}=1$. Thus it can serve as a dimensionless argument if a separately specified model assigns it as a phase; this dimensional calculation alone proves no frame-transformation or covariance law. Combining with steps 1.1-1.5, every quantity and displayed law checked here is dimensionally consistent under the stated conventions.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Recall that $T_{u,v}\in\mathcal B(H)$ denotes the rank-one operator $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]).

(a) A **density operator** on $H$ is a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). If $(u_n)_{n\in J}$ is a finite or countable orthonormal family, with $J$ a finite initial segment of the positive integers or all positive integers, and $w_n\ge0$ with $\sum_nw_n=1$, then the sum $\rho:=\sum_nw_nT_{u_n,u_n}$ converges in trace norm to a density operator with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=\sum_nw_n=1$. Conversely every density operator $\rho$ admits such an expansion whose weights are its positive eigenvalues counted with multiplicity and whose vectors are orthonormal eigenvectors; distinct expansions of the same $\rho$ exist when a positive eigenspace has dimension at least two.

(b) Let $E$ be a projection-valued measure on a measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ acting on $H$ ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]). Then $\mu_\rho(B):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E(B))$ is a well-defined probability measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ ([[def-measure]], [[def-probability-measure]]); it is given by the absolutely convergent series $\mu_\rho(B)=\sum_nw_n\|E(B)u_n\|^2$ in every expansion of (a), and reduces to $\mu_\rho(B)=\|E(B)u\|^2$ for a pure density operator $\rho=T_{u,u}$ with $\|u\|=1$.

(c) Assume in addition the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator with projection-valued measure $E_A$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let $\psi\in H$ have $\|\psi\|=1$ and $\psi\in D(A)$. Then

$$\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\|A\psi\|^2 ,$$

where $E_{A,\psi}(B)=\langle E_A(B)\psi,\psi\rangle$ ([[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]); moreover $\int_{\mathbb R}|\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)<\infty$ exactly when $\psi\in D(|A|^{1/2})$, and then the mean $\int\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}$ is finite. No product $A\rho$ of an unbounded operator with a density operator is used, and no physical interpretation of $\mu_\rho$ or of the moments is asserted.

Bounded tensor maps act on product vectors by $S\otimes T(\psi_{A}\otimes\psi_{B})=(S\psi_{A})\otimes(T\psi_{B})$, and $(S\otimes T)^*=S^*\otimes T^*$; hence tensoring the self-adjoint $S_z$ with $I$ gives a bounded self-adjoint operator ([[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]] clauses (a), (c)).

Let $s\in\frac12\mathbb N=\{0,\tfrac12,1,\tfrac32,\dots\}$, put $N:=2s\in\mathbb N$ and let
$V_s:=\mathbb C^{N+1}$ carry the standard inner product
$\langle z,w\rangle=\sum_{k=0}^{N}z_k\overline{w_k}$, linear in the first argument
([[def-inner-product-space]]). Write $(e_m)_{-s\le m\le s}$ for the standard basis, indexed so that
$e_m$ is the vector with entry $1$ in position $k=s-m$ and entry $0$ elsewhere; thus
$\langle e_m,e_n\rangle=1$ if $m=n$ and $\langle e_m,e_n\rangle=0$ otherwise. Define $\mathbb C$-linear maps
$J_z,J_+,J_-\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V_s)$ by their values on this basis ([[def-linear-map]]):

$$J_ze_m:=m\,e_m,\qquad J_+e_m:=\sqrt{(s-m)(s+m+1)}\,e_{m+1},\qquad J_-e_m:=\sqrt{(s+m)(s-m+1)}\,e_{m-1},$$

where $e_{s+1}:=0$ and $e_{-s-1}:=0$, and put

$$J_x:=\tfrac12(J_++J_-),\qquad J_y:=\tfrac1{2i}(J_+-J_-),\qquad J^2:=J_x^2+J_y^2+J_z^2 .$$

Then:

(a) $J_z$, $J_x$ and $J_y$ are self-adjoint endomorphisms of $V_s$
([[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]]), and $J_+^*=J_-$, $J_-^*=J_+$
([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]]);

(b) on $V_s$ the commutators are

$$[J_z,J_+]=J_+,\qquad [J_z,J_-]=-J_-,\qquad [J_+,J_-]=2J_z,\qquad [J_x,J_y]=iJ_z,\qquad [J_y,J_z]=iJ_x,\qquad [J_z,J_x]=iJ_y ;$$

(c) $J^2=J_-J_++J_z^2+J_z=J_+J_-+J_z^2-J_z=s(s+1)I$, and $[J^2,J_z]=[J^2,J_\pm]=0$;

(d) the matrix elements of the raising operator are
$\|J_+e_m\|^2=(s-m)(s+m+1)$ and $\|J_-e_m\|^2=(s+m)(s-m+1)$, and
$\langle J_+e_m,e_{m+1}\rangle=\sqrt{(s-m)(s+m+1)}$, which is nonzero exactly when $m<s$;

(e) for $s=\tfrac12$, identify $V_{\frac12}=\mathbb C^2$ with the basis ordered as $(e_{\frac12},e_{-\frac12})$ and let

$$\sigma_x:=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_y:=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\ i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_z:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$$

be the Pauli matrices. Then $J_i=\tfrac12\sigma_i$ for $i=x,y,z$, $\sigma_x^2=\sigma_y^2=\sigma_z^2=I$,
$\sigma_x\sigma_y=i\sigma_z$, $\sigma_y\sigma_z=i\sigma_x$, $\sigma_z\sigma_x=i\sigma_y$, and consequently
$\sigma_i\sigma_j+\sigma_j\sigma_i=2\delta_{ij}I$ and $\sigma_i\sigma_j=\delta_{ij}I+i\sum_k\varepsilon_{ijk}\sigma_k$ for all $i,j$, where $\delta_{ij}=1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise, and $\varepsilon_{ijk}$ denotes the sign of the permutation $(x,y,z)\mapsto(i,j,k)$.

All statements are finite-dimensional linear algebra: no physical interpretation of $J_x,J_y,J_z$ as angular momentum, and no measurement postulate, is asserted here.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following statements about sharp and unsharp real-valued quantities. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The latter is the explicit hypothesis used to obtain the spectral PVM of a general self-adjoint operator from [[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]] in clause (ii); consumers invoking this construction inherit it.

**(i) Sharp observables.** An **ideal sharp real-valued quantity** (observable) of a system with state space $H$ is a densely defined self-adjoint operator $A:D(A)\subset H\to H$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]), together with a declared unit in which its real spectral coordinate is read; the unit is part of the assignment, and no numerical value of the coordinate is asserted by the assignment. Symmetry of $A$ on a small domain is not sufficient for self-adjointness, and the domain is a declared part of the observable.

**(ii) Spectral probability.** Let $E_{A}$ be the spectral projection-valued measure of the self-adjoint operator $A$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], [[def-projection-valued-measure]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). For a preparation $\rho$ and a Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R$ the **probability of the outcome in $B$** is
$$\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\rho\,E_{A}(B)\bigr),\qquad\text{and for a pure preparation }[\psi]\text{ it is }\mu^{A}_{\psi}(B)=\|E_{A}(B)\psi\|^{2}.$$
By clause (b) of [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] the assignment $B\mapsto\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B)$ is a probability measure on the Borel sets ([[def-probability-measure]], [[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]). It is the general form of the Born rule adopted here.

**(iii) Nature of the outcome law.** The probability law is a measure, not necessarily a density with respect to Lebesgue measure and not necessarily a finite or countable sum of point masses: a self-adjoint operator with continuous spectrum ordinarily has no normalizable eigenvector at a point of its continuous spectrum, so an "exact value" of a continuum quantity is not represented by a normalized state. An ideal point value is an idealization; a real detector reports a finite-resolution outcome, that is, the probability of a declared Borel set $B$ such as a bin, and the recorded-event probability is that of (ii) for the bin, not the value of a density at a point.

**(iv) Unsharp finite outcomes.** Outcomes of a finite-resolution apparatus with finitely many channels are described, when the idealization uses bounded effects, by a finite family $(F_{a})_{a=1}^{p}$ of bounded operators with $0\le F_{a}\le I$ in the quadratic-form order and $\sum_{a}F_{a}=I$ ([[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]), the **outcome probabilities** being $p_{a}=\operatorname{tr}(\rho F_{a})$. They are normalized for every state space assigned by P1, as shown by the preceding general-H calculation. This unsharp extension is an operational description tied to an apparatus model; it is not obtained from the sharp observable by mathematical manipulation alone, and the effects alone do not determine what happens to the state after the outcome (P3).

**(v) Moments are a separate matter.** Statements about the mean, variance or higher moments of the outcome law require the corresponding integrability of $t\mapsto t^{n}$ against $\mu^{A}_{\rho}$ and are not part of this postulate; where they are used they are stated with their hypotheses. In particular the existence of $\operatorname{tr}(\rho A)$ for an unbounded $A$ is not asserted.

**(vi) Status.** Clauses (i)-(v) are adopted assumptions of the model. They assert nothing about which quantities of a concrete apparatus are sharp, about the physical mechanism producing an outcome or about the completeness of the description; a laboratory record is a classical event whose relation to the model is a tested identification with uncertainty, in the sense of P7.

derivations.claim: Let $\psi:=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(e_{+}+e_{-})$, so $\|\psi\|=1$ by orthonormality. The pure preparation is the unit ray $[\psi]=\{z\psi:z\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}\}$: the vector $e^{i\theta}\psi$ has the same norm and defines the same ray, and the associated density operator $T_{\psi,\psi}$ satisfies $\operatorname{tr}T_{\psi,\psi}=\|\psi\|^{2}=1$ by [L2]; hence it is a density operator in the sense of [L1].

Let $0<w<1$ and let $\psi_{1},\psi_{2}$ be orthonormal vectors of $H$, and put $\rho:=w\,T_{\psi_{1},\psi_{1}}+(1-w)T_{\psi_{2},\psi_{2}}$. By [L1] $\rho$ is a density operator with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=w+(1-w)=1$; orthogonality gives $\rho\psi_{1}=w\psi_{1}$ and $\rho\psi_{2}=(1-w)\psi_{2}$. Both eigenvalues are positive, so the range of $\rho$ contains the two linearly independent vectors $\psi_1,\psi_2$; hence $\rho$ has rank at least two and is not a rank-one operator $T_{\varphi,\varphi}$ for any $\varphi$. The mixture of two orthogonal pure preparations is therefore a preparation of a different type from either component.

On the composite $H\widehat\otimes H$ consider the product state $\Psi:=e_{+}\otimes e_{+}$ and the local observable $S_{z}\otimes I$. By [L3] and the self-adjointness of $S_z$ in [L4], this tensor operator is self-adjoint, and $(S_{z}\otimes I)\Psi=(S_{z}e_{+})\otimes e_{+}=\tfrac{\hbar}{2}\,\Psi$. On the product basis of $H\widehat\otimes H$, the spectral projection for $\hbar/2$ is $P_{+}\otimes I$, so the local outcome probability for $\{\hbar/2\}$ is $\|(P_{+}\otimes I)\Psi\|^{2}=1$.

For the state $\psi=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(e_{+}+e_{-})$ the outcome law of $S_{z}$ is $B\mapsto\mu^{S_{z}}_{\psi}(B)=\operatorname{tr}(T_{\psi,\psi}E_{S_{z}}(B))=\|E_{S_{z}}(B)\psi\|^{2}$. By [L4] the projections are $P_{\pm}$ onto the lines $\mathbb Ce_{\pm}$, so $\mu^{S_{z}}_{\psi}(\{\hbar/2\})=\|P_{+}\psi\|^{2}=\tfrac12$ and $\mu^{S_{z}}_{\psi}(\{-\hbar/2\})=\|P_{-}\psi\|^{2}=\tfrac12$. Thus the law is $\tfrac12\delta_{\hbar/2}+\tfrac12\delta_{-\hbar/2}$ on the two-point set $\sigma(S_{z})$ and is not concentrated at a single outcome; its finite mean is $\tfrac12(\hbar/2)+\tfrac12(-\hbar/2)=0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), let $d\ge1$ and work on $H=L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ ([[def-hilbert-space]]).

(a) For a real measurable finite-valued function $a:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ define $M_af:=af$ on $D(M_a):=\{f\in H: af\in H\}$. Then $M_a$ is a densely defined self-adjoint operator on $H$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]).

(b) Let $c>0$, $b\in\mathbb R$, and let $\mathcal F_2$ be the unitary Plancherel transform with the convention $\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}dx$ on $L^1$ ([[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]], [[thm-plancherel]]). Define

$$H_0:=\mathcal F_2^*\,M_{c|\xi|^2+b}\,\mathcal F_2,\qquad D(H_0):=\{f\in H:|\xi|^2\mathcal F_2f\in H\}.$$

Then $H_0$ is self-adjoint, $D(H_0)$ coincides with the Sobolev space $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ as a set (with equivalent norms, [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[thm-fourier-characterisation-of-integer-order-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]]), $H_0\ge b$ in the quadratic-form sense, and for every Schwartz function $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, $H_0f=-(c/4\pi^2)\Delta f+bf$.

(c) If $V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ is measurable with $\|V\|_\infty<\infty$ and $H:=H_0+M_V$ with domain $D(H_0)$, then $H$ is self-adjoint on $D(H_0)$, is bounded below, and the assignment $t\mapsto e^{itH}$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group whose generator is $iH$: the limit $\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t(e^{itH}\psi-\psi)$ exists exactly for $\psi\in D(H)$ and equals $iH\psi$ ([[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]]).

(d) *Scope*: the argument uses only boundedness and measurability of $V$; it proves nothing for $V\propto-1/|x|$, $V\propto|x|^2$ or the delta interaction, does not identify $H_0$ with any measured free-particle Hamiltonian, and asserts no physical interpretation.

Fix an integer $n\ge1$. With the complex smooth-function convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]] and multi-indices of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], define
$$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|,\qquad \mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)=\{f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C):p_{\alpha\beta}(f)<\infty\text{ for all }\alpha,\beta\}.$$
The zero multi-index gives $x^0=1$ and $\partial^0f=f$. These are actual smooth functions, not equivalence classes. The notation $C_c^\infty$ uses the support convention in [[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]].

Pointwise differentiation is linear; thus $p_{\alpha\beta}(f+g)\le p_{\alpha\beta}(f)+p_{\alpha\beta}(g)$ and $p_{\alpha\beta}(cf)=|c|p_{\alpha\beta}(f)$. In particular this set is a complex vector space and each $p_{\alpha\beta}$ is a seminorm. The zero function belongs to it. Since $p_{00}(f)=0$ forces $f(x)=0$ for every $x$, the family separates functions. No choice principle is needed.

(b) For every $j$, $P_j$ is self-adjoint with domain
$$D(P_j)=\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C):\ \xi_j\mathcal F_2f\in L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)\},$$
and for every $f\in D(P_j)$, $\mathcal F_2(P_jf)(\xi)=2\pi\hbar\,\xi_j\,\mathcal F_2f(\xi)$
for almost every $\xi$. In particular $P_jf=-i\hbar D_jf$ for every
$f\in W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$, and for $d=1$ the domain of the single
momentum operator is exactly $D(P)=W^{1,2}(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix
$\hbar>0$ and an integer $d\ge1$, and work in the complex Hilbert space
$L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with inner product
$\langle f,g\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R^d}f\overline g$ linear in the first
argument ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]],
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]).

**Weak derivatives.** For $f\in L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ and
$j\in\{1,\dots,d\}$, say that the $j$-th weak derivative of $f$ exists in
$L^2$ when there is a class $g\in L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with
$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}f\,D_j\varphi=(-1)\int_{\mathbb R^d}g\,\varphi \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d),$$
where $D_j\varphi$ is the classical partial derivative and the pairing is
bilinear without conjugation ([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]).
Such a $g$ is unique as an $L^2$ class
([[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]]); write $D_jf:=g$.
The Sobolev space $W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ is the set of classes
$f\in L^2$ for which $D_1f,\dots,D_df$ all exist in $L^2$, and
$W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ is the set of $f\in W^{1,2}$ with
$D_jf\in W^{1,2}$ for every $j$, with $D_jD_kf$ written for the iterated
derivative ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]).

**(a) Position operators.** For $j\in\{1,\dots,d\}$ define
$$D(Q_j):=\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C):\ x\mapsto x_jf(x)\in L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)\},\qquad (Q_jf)(x):=x_jf(x).$$
Thus $Q_jf$ is the class of the pointwise product with the $j$-th coordinate
function.

**(b) Momentum operators.** For $j\in\{1,\dots,d\}$ define
$$D(P_j):=\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C):\ D_jf\text{ exists in }L^2\},\qquad P_jf:=-i\hbar\,D_jf .$$

Both $Q_j$ and $P_j$ are densely defined $\mathbb C$-linear operators in
$L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$: for $Q_j$ the compactly supported smooth
classes lie in the domain because $x_j$ is bounded there, and for $P_j$ they
lie in the domain because their classical derivatives are weak derivatives in
$L^2$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]). For a class
$f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ one has $Q_jf=x_jf$ and
$P_jf=-i\hbar\,\partial_jf$ pointwise. The self-adjointness of these operators
and their Fourier representation are proved in
the companion self-adjointness lemma on this page, not
asserted here; for $d=1$ the domain $D(P)$ of the single momentum operator
coincides with $W^{1,2}(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following kinematics and one-particle model. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), which are the choice hypotheses of the cited operator suppliers.

**(i) Spacetime and frames.** The model reads its events and frames in the Newtonian arena of [[def-nrqm-framework-newtonian-spacetime]], with inertial frames and frame changes as in [[def-nrqm-framework-inertial-frames]]: the frame changes are the Galilean transformations of [[def-nrqm-framework-galilei-transformations]], and their composition is governed by the group law of [[lem-nrqm-framework-galilei-transformations-form-a-group]]. derivations.claim: [No strong limit on a smooth class] Take the normalized $\psi_{L_0}\in C_c^{\infty}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ of [L3], for which $\Delta\psi_{L_0}\ne0$. By [L1], $K_m\psi_{L_0}=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\Delta\psi_{L_0}$, so $\|K_m\psi_{L_0}\|_2=\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\|\Delta\psi_{L_0}\|_2\to+\infty$ as $m\downarrow0$. Therefore this family is not Cauchy in $L^2$ on this Schwartz vector and cannot converge there to $K_0\psi_{L_0}$ for any operator $K_0$; in particular it cannot converge on every Schwartz state.

[Every fixed state with nonzero momentum second moment has divergent kinetic expectation] Let $\psi\in W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ be fixed and normalized, and suppose $p_2(\psi):=\sum_j\|P_j\psi\|_2^2>0$. Each first weak derivative of $\psi$ lies in $L^2$ by its $W^{2,2}$ membership, so [L2] places $\psi$ in every $D(P_j)$ and makes each $\|P_j\psi\|_2^2$ finite. For each mass $m>0$, its model root-mean-square speed is $v_{\mathrm{rms},m}(\psi):=m^{-1}p_2(\psi)^{1/2}$, which is finite and nonzero; this speed is not held fixed when $m$ varies. By [L5], its kinetic expectation is $\langle K_m\psi,\psi\rangle=p_2(\psi)/(2m)\to+\infty$ as $m\downarrow0$. Thus the claimed divergence holds for exactly the stated fixed-state class, with no claim for vectors outside this operator domain.

[Frequency divergence] By [L4], $[\hbar|k|^{2}/m]=\tau^{-1}$, and for each fixed wave number $k\ne0$ the formal free frequency $\omega_m(k)=\frac{\hbar|k|^2}{2m}$ satisfies $\omega_m(k)\to+\infty$ as $m\downarrow0$. Thus no finite frequency law arises at a fixed nonzero wave number in this limit, and in particular it does not produce a law linear in $|k|$.

Step 1.1 refutes the asserted strong convergence for every Schwartz state, step 1.2 establishes divergence for the stated nonzero-velocity class, and step 1.3 refutes a finite limiting frequency at each fixed nonzero wave number. Hence the mass-zero limiting inference fails for the displayed massive family; this does not rule out a separately specified massless model.

Let $M_3(\mathbb R)$ be the set of $3\times3$ matrices over $\mathbb R$ ([[def-matrix-space]]), with identity $I_3$ and product as in [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], transpose $R^{\mathsf T}$ as in [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]], and determinant $\det R$ as in [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]].

The **orthogonal group** and the **special orthogonal group** are the subsets

$$O(3):=\{R\in M_3(\mathbb R):R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3\},\qquad SO(3):=\{R\in M_3(\mathbb R):R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3\ \text{and}\ \det R=1\}.$$

Equivalently $SO(3)=O(3)\cap\{R:\det R=1\}$. Elements of $SO(3)$ are called **rotations**. The identification of $M_3(\mathbb R)$ with the function space $\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ and hence with $\mathbb R^9$ is the one of [[def-matrix-space]]; when $M_3(\mathbb R)$ is regarded as a metric or topological space, this is always the Euclidean metric of that identification.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and vector-valued functions, their
components and their limits are as in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]].

### The derivative

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be
a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of
$f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$

the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of
$A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of
$f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by

Let $f$ be Riemann integrable on every compact interval $[a,R]$ with $R>a$. The improper integral over the right-unbounded interval is
$$\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx:=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_a^R f(x)\,dx,$$
provided this limit exists as a finite real number. In that case the improper integral **converges**; otherwise it diverges. In particular, a limit of $+\infty$ or $-\infty$ is divergence, not convergence to an extended-real value.

If $f$ is Riemann integrable on every $[R,b]$ with $R<b$, define
$$\int_{-\infty}^b f(x)\,dx:=\lim_{R\to-\infty}\int_R^b f(x)\,dx$$
under the same finite-limit convention. All finite integrals use the oriented convention.

For every rational $p$,
$$\int_1^\infty x^{-p}\,dx\ \text{converges exactly when }p>1,$$
and
$$\int_0^1 x^{-p}\,dx\ \text{converges exactly when }p<1.$$
When they converge, their values are respectively $1/(p-1)$ and $1/(1-p)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

- For $0<p<\infty$, define an equivalence relation on $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ by
  $$f\sim g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f-g\in\mathcal N(\mu),$$
  and write $L^p(\mu)$ for the set of classes $[f]$.
- For $p=\infty$, define the same relation on $L^\infty(\mu)$ and again write
  $L^\infty(\mu)$ for the set of classes.

Thus an element of $L^p(\mu)$ is an almost-everywhere equivalence class of
measurable representatives.

When $1\le p\le\infty$, the displayed set quotient agrees with the usual
quotient-vector-space construction of
[[def-quotient-vector-space-and-canonical-projection]].

For $0<p<1$, the same class notation is used; under its stated choice hypothesis, the later item
[[thm-the-l-p-distance-for-zero-less-p-less-one-is-a-complete-translation-invariant-metric]]
supplies the metric structure rather than a normed-space structure.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex with at least two elements
([[def-interval]]) and let $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Call $G : I \to \mathbb{R}$ a **primitive of $f$ on
$I$** when $G$ is differentiable at every point of $I$ as a function on $I$ with
$G' = f$ there ([[def-derivative]]). Then:

1. **Existence.** Fix $c_0 \in I$. The function
   $$F : I \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad F(x) \;:=\; \int_{c_0}^x f$$
   is defined at every $x \in I$ ([[def-oriented-integral]],
   [[def-the-integral-function]]) and is a primitive of $f$ on $I$.
2. **Uniqueness up to a constant.** If $G_1$ and $G_2$ are primitives of $f$ on
   $I$ then there is a real $k$ with $G_1(x) = G_2(x) + k$ for every $x \in I$.
3. **Evaluation.** If $a, b \in I$ with $a < b$ and $G$ is any primitive of $f$
   on $I$, then
   $$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**The scope is exactly the continuous case, and that is not a limitation of the
proof.** An integrable function need not have a primitive, and a function with a
primitive need not be integrable; this corollary is precisely the intersection
where both fundamental theorems apply, and both witnesses are on the companion
page.

Powers are those of [[def-integer-power]], and $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to
\mathbb{R}$ is the canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]], so that
$\iota(0) = 0$ and $\iota(m+1) = \iota(m) + 1$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

1. The function $p_0 : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $p_0(x) = x^{0}$, is the
   constant function $1$, and it is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$
   with $p_0'(c) = 0$ ([[def-derivative]]).
2. For $n \ge 1$ the function $p_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$,
   $p_n(x) = x^{n}$, is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and
   $$p_n'(c) \;=\; \iota(n)\,c^{\,n-1} .$$
3. For $n \ge 1$ put $A_0 := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ne 0 \,\}$. The function
   $m_n : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $m_n(x) = x^{-n}$, is differentiable at every
   $c \in A_0$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$m_n'(c) \;=\; -\,\iota(n)\,c^{\,-n-1} .$$
4. Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $a_j = 0$ for $j \ge n$, and let
   $P : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the polynomial function
   $P(x) = \sum_{j<n} a_j x^{j}$ ([[def-finite-sum]]). Then $P$ is
   differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and, defining $e : \mathbb{N}
   \to \mathbb{R}$ by $e_0 := 0$ and $e_j := \iota(j)\,a_j\,c^{\,j-1}$ for
   $j \ge 1$,
   $$P'(c) \;=\; \sum_{j<n} e_j .$$

**Claim 2 is stated for $n \ge 1$ and not for $n \ge 0$, and that is not
timidity.** At $n = 0$ its right-hand side reads $\iota(0)\,c^{-1}$, and
$c^{-1}$ is not defined at $c = 0$ ([[def-integer-power]]), so the formula is
not a statement about the whole line. Claim 1 is what covers $n = 0$, and it
says the derivative is $0$ there, which is what the informal reading
"$0 \cdot c^{-1}$" is reaching for. The same shift is why the term $e_0$ of
claim 4 is defined to be $0$ outright rather than by the formula.

Let $f$ be Riemann integrable on every compact interval $[a,R]$ with $R>a$. The improper integral over the right-unbounded interval is
$$\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx:=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_a^R f(x)\,dx,$$
provided this limit exists as a finite real number. In that case the improper integral **converges**; otherwise it diverges. In particular, a limit of $+\infty$ or $-\infty$ is divergence, not convergence to an extended-real value.

If $f$ is Riemann integrable on every $[R,b]$ with $R<b$, define
$$\int_{-\infty}^b f(x)\,dx:=\lim_{R\to-\infty}\int_R^b f(x)\,dx$$
under the same finite-limit convention. All finite integrals use the oriented convention.

for every $x$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix
$\hbar>0$ and an integer $d\ge1$, and work in the complex Hilbert space
$L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with inner product
$\langle f,g\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R^d}f\overline g$ linear in the first
argument ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]],
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]).

**Weak derivatives.** For $f\in L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ and
$j\in\{1,\dots,d\}$, say that the $j$-th weak derivative of $f$ exists in
$L^2$ when there is a class $g\in L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with
$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}f\,D_j\varphi=(-1)\int_{\mathbb R^d}g\,\varphi \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d),$$
where $D_j\varphi$ is the classical partial derivative and the pairing is
bilinear without conjugation ([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]).
Such a $g$ is unique as an $L^2$ class
([[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]]); write $D_jf:=g$.
The Sobolev space $W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ is the set of classes
$f\in L^2$ for which $D_1f,\dots,D_df$ all exist in $L^2$, and
$W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ is the set of $f\in W^{1,2}$ with
$D_jf\in W^{1,2}$ for every $j$, with $D_jD_kf$ written for the iterated
derivative ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]).

**(a) Position operators.** For $j\in\{1,\dots,d\}$ define
$$D(Q_j):=\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C):\ x\mapsto x_jf(x)\in L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)\},\qquad (Q_jf)(x):=x_jf(x).$$
Thus $Q_jf$ is the class of the pointwise product with the $j$-th coordinate
function.

**(b) Momentum operators.** For $j\in\{1,\dots,d\}$ define
$$D(P_j):=\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C):\ D_jf\text{ exists in }L^2\},\qquad P_jf:=-i\hbar\,D_jf .$$

Both $Q_j$ and $P_j$ are densely defined $\mathbb C$-linear operators in
$L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$: for $Q_j$ the compactly supported smooth
classes lie in the domain because $x_j$ is bounded there, and for $P_j$ they
lie in the domain because their classical derivatives are weak derivatives in
$L^2$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]). For a class
$f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ one has $Q_jf=x_jf$ and
$P_jf=-i\hbar\,\partial_jf$ pointwise. The self-adjointness of these operators
and their Fourier representation are proved in
the companion self-adjointness lemma on this page, not
asserted here; for $d=1$ the domain $D(P)$ of the single momentum operator
coincides with $W^{1,2}(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

derivations.claim: [Norm one] The squared modulus is $1/(4L_0)$ on $[-L_0,L_0]$ and $L_0/(4x^2)$ for $|x|\ge L_0$. Its integral is $2L_0/(4L_0)+2\int_{L_0}^{\infty}L_0/(4x^2)\,dx=\tfrac12+\tfrac{L_0}{2}\lim_{N\to\infty}(L_0^{-1}-N^{-1})=1$ by [L2] and [L3], so $\psi_{L_0}$ is a normalized state.

[Second moment infinite] The second moment is $\int_{\mathbb R}x^{2}|\psi_{L_0}|^{2}\,dx=\frac{L_0^2}{6}+2\int_{L_0}^{\infty}x^{2}\cdot\frac{L_0}{4x^{2}}\,dx=\frac{L_0^2}{6}+\frac{L_0}{2}\lim_{N\to\infty}(N-L_0)=+\infty$ by [L2] and [L3]; equivalently $x\psi_{L_0}\notin L^{2}$ and $\psi_{L_0}\notin D(Q)$, although it is a normalized state.

[First absolute moment infinite] The first absolute moment is $\int_{\mathbb R}|x|\,|\psi_{L_0}|^{2}\,dx=\frac{L_0}{4}+2\int_{L_0}^{\infty}x\cdot\frac{L_0}{4x^{2}}\,dx=\frac{L_0}{4}+\frac{L_0}{2}\lim_{N\to\infty}\ln(N/L_0)=+\infty$ by [L2] and [L3]. Both one-sided integrals diverge, so $x$ is not integrable for the probability measure $\mu_{\psi_{L_0}}^Q$ and its Lebesgue expectation is not a finite real mean.

By steps 1.1-1.3 the P1 preparation $[\psi_{L_0}]$ is normalized and its P2 position law has infinite first absolute moment, so the refuted universal claim fails.
